summary: Specifies an experimental ICMPv6 message type for the Identifier-Locator Network Protocol (ILNP). The message dynamically updates identifier and locator bindings for an existing ILNP session. It comes from the IRTF Routing Research Group.

eli5.summary: If you move to a new house, you send a note to your pen pal with your new address. This message does that for a computer during a conversation. It is only an experiment.

questions: what is the ilnpv6 locator update message
how does ilnpv6 handle node mobility
what icmp type is used for locator updates
subtitle: A message that lets a moving IPv6 node tell others about its new locations.

tldr.problem: In ILNP, a node's locator can change when it moves or gains a new network connection, but its correspondents need to know about these changes to keep sending packets to the right place.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 6743 defines a new ICMPv6 message type (156) that carries a list of valid locators, preferences, and lifetimes, which a node sends to all of its active conversation partners whenever its locator set changes.
tldr.outcome: ILNPv6 nodes can seamlessly notify correspondents of location changes, enabling transparent mobility without breaking existing sessions.

today: RFC 6743 is an Experimental Protocol. It defines a message type used only by ILNP implementations, which have not seen wide deployment.

sections.title: Introduction and Design Rationale
sections.content:
The Identifier-Locator Network Protocol for IPv6 (ILNPv6) decouples a node's identity from its location. A node can change its locator when it moves between networks or adds a new network connection, but conversations with other nodes should continue without interruption. To achieve this, a node must inform its conversation partners of the new set of valid locators it can be reached at.

Rather than waiting for DNS to be updated (which takes time), ILNP uses a dedicated control message. This RFC defines the ICMPv6 Locator Update message, which efficiently communicates locator changes directly between ILNP nodes. The message is sent only for ILNPv6 sessions and always requires authentication via the Nonce Option to prevent forged updates.
sections.eli5: When a node moves, it sends a special control message to say 'I am still me, but I have a new address.' The message lists all the places you can reach this node now, and which ones are preferred.

sections.title: Locator Update Message Structure
sections.content:
The ICMPv6 Locator Update message has Type 156 and includes a Type, Code, Checksum, and a body containing:

  • Num of Locs: The count of 64-bit locator values in the message (must not be zero).
  • Operation: Either Advertisement (0x01) when announcing new locators, or Acknowledgement (0x02) when confirming receipt.
  • RESERVED: A field held for future use, currently set to zero.
  • Locator values: One or more 64-bit locators the sending node is currently valid at.
  • Preference: A 16-bit value for each locator indicating relative preference (lower is preferred).
  • Lifetime: The maximum number of seconds each locator is valid.

The message follows the standard ICMPv6 checksum calculation.
sections.eli5: The message says 'here are all my valid addresses, here is which one I prefer, and here is how long each one is good for.' It works like an ICMP error message but carries locator data instead.

sections.title: Session Update Behavior
sections.content:
When a node's set of valid locators changes, it MUST send a Locator Update Advertisement to each correspondent node it has an active ILNP session with. The Advertisement lists all currently valid locators. A receiver of a valid Advertisement MUST send back a Locator Update Acknowledgement with identical content except for the Operation field.

All ILNPv6 Locator Update messages MUST contain a valid ILNPv6 Identifier option and MUST contain an ILNPv6 Nonce Option. These protect against forgeries and verify that the node actually supports ILNP. Implementations must support a large number of locator values in a single message, since a multihomed node or site might have many locators.
sections.eli5: When you move, you send out the new address list and wait for people to say 'got it.' The message is signed with a secret stamp (the nonce) so people know it really came from you.

sections.title: Security and Authentication
sections.content:
The ILNP Nonce Destination Option (defined in RFC 6744) MUST be present in packets containing a Locator Update message. The receiver MUST verify that the nonce value is correct before accepting the update. If either condition fails, the packet is discarded as a forgery and a security event is logged.

ILNP sessions operating in higher-threat environments SHOULD also use IP Security (IPsec) in addition to the nonce protection. The nonce option MUST still be present even when IPsec is in use. Implementations must handle large numbers of locators without developing security faults like stack overflow.
sections.eli5: The nonce is like a secret password on each message. You check the nonce before believing the locator change is real. For really important systems, you can also encrypt the whole message with IPsec.

sections.title: Compatibility with Standard IPv6
sections.content:
When ILNPv6 is not in use, receiving IPv6 nodes MUST discard the ICMP Locator Update packet without processing it. This is standard behavior for any non-ILNPv6 node receiving an ICMPv6 message with an unknown type value. The message has no impact on transport-layer protocols.

The message may affect where packets for a transport-layer session are sent, but ILNP's design goal is to decouple transport-layer sessions from network-layer location changes. This message enables that decoupling by notifying correspondents of new locators before any session disruption occurs.
sections.eli5: Older computers that do not know about ILNPv6 will just ignore this message. It does not break anything on the regular internet.

fields.name: Checksum
fields.desc: One's complement checksum of the message.

fields.name: Num of Locs
fields.desc: Number of locator values (must not be zero).
